lead: Supercharging forces more air mass into the same swept volume. More trapped air allows more fuel, so a smaller engine can give the power of a larger one. The blower is driven from the crankshaft, so it costs engine power; the useful figure is the net gain. Superchargers appear in performance petrol cars, aircraft at altitude, and some industrial diesels. This chapter covers the objectives, the main mechanical types, the density ratio, and the effects on knock, thermal load and exhaust. Exhaust-driven boosting follows in Turbocharging methods and turbo lag.
prereq: You need: swept volume and volumetric efficiency from engine terminology, and knock from abnormal combustion in SI engines; charge cooling is in Variable geometry turbochargers and intercooling.

blocks.text: A naturally aspirated engine fills the cylinder with air near ambient pressure, about 1.0 bar. Its torque is limited by the air mass trapped each cycle. A supercharger raises the intake pressure above ambient; the ratio p₂/p₁ is the pressure ratio, using absolute pressures. The mass trapped also depends on temperature: hot air is less dense. For a perfect gas, density ratio is pressure ratio times the inverse temperature ratio. A boost to 1.6 bar sounds like 60 percent more air. But compression heats the air: even a perfect (isentropic) compressor takes 300 K air to T₂ = T₁ (p₂/p₁)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup> = 300 × 1.6<sup>0.286</sup> = 343 K, and a real one with isentropic efficiency η<sub>c</sub> = 0.70 reaches T₂ = T₁ + (343 − 300)/η<sub>c</sub> = 362 K. The density ratio is then only (1.6/1.0) × (300/362) = 1.33, about 33 percent more air.

blocks.where: ρ is density in kg/m³; p is absolute pressure; T is absolute temperature in K; subscript 1 is ambient before the blower, subscript 2 is after the blower.

items: More power for the same swept volume and better power-to-weight ratio.
Altitude compensation: a blower restores sea-level air density when ambient pressure falls.
Sometimes lower specific fuel consumption, because friction and engine weight are spread over more kW.

blocks.text: All mechanical superchargers are driven by a belt or gears from the crankshaft. The roots blower has two rotors, each with two or three lobes, turning in opposite directions inside a close-fitting casing. Each lobe traps a pocket of air at inlet pressure and carries it round the outside to the delivery side. There is no compression inside the blower: the pressure rises only when the pocket opens to the higher-pressure manifold and air flows back into it, which makes the roots blower hotter and less efficient at high pressure ratio than a compressing machine. It is a positive-displacement machine: flow per revolution is nearly constant, so the air delivered rises with engine speed. The sliding-vane blower uses vanes in a rotor to trap and move air; it is simple but the vanes wear. The centrifugal blower uses a fast impeller to throw air outward; pressure rises roughly with tip speed squared. It is efficient at high speed but gives little boost at low speed.

Positive-displacement blowers give strong low-speed response. Centrifugal blowers suit high-speed power. The figure follows the worked example through a belt-driven roots blower: the pressure rises 1.6 times, but the temperature rises too, so the density rises only 1.33 times.

sections.h3: Drive power and the net gain

blocks.text: The blower takes power from the crank. The honest output is net brake power: P<sub>net</sub> = P<sub>gross</sub> − P<sub>drive</sub>, where P<sub>gross</sub> is the power from the extra trapped air and P<sub>drive</sub> is the compressor work plus belt and gear losses. P<sub>drive</sub> often reaches 10 to 20 percent of gross power at high boost. The drive power is the compressor work plus the drive losses: P<sub>drive</sub> = ṁ<sub>a</sub> c<sub>p</sub> (T₂ − T₁) ÷ η<sub>drive</sub>, where ṁ<sub>a</sub> is the air mass flow in kg/s, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K for air and η<sub>drive</sub> the belt and gear efficiency. Drive power grows with mass flow and with pressure ratio, and so does charge heating. That sets the limits of supercharging: the net gain is always smaller than the density ratio suggests, and knock and thermal load grow with boost.

items: Peak cylinder pressure and temperature rise, so pistons, valves, head gasket and bearings face higher thermal and mechanical load. Cooling and lubrication must be upgraded.

In SI engines, boost raises end-gas pressure and temperature, so knock tendency rises. Common fixes are a lower compression ratio, higher-octane fuel, retarded spark and charge cooling; see Variable geometry turbochargers and intercooling.
In CI engines, more air mass reduces smoke at a given fuel rate, but higher temperature can raise NOx; injection timing may need adjustment.

Exhaust mass flow rises with boost. Exhaust temperature does not always rise: in a CI engine the extra air usually lowers it at the same fuel rate, while in an SI engine it depends on the mixture and timing. The exhaust manifold must withstand the greater heat flow, and back pressure must stay low enough for good scavenging.

Modifications for supercharging include lower compression ratio, stronger pistons and gasket, larger cooling and oil capacity, fuel enrichment and intercooling. A blower is not a simple bolt-on for a standard engine.
Emissions change: more power per litre, but higher NOx is possible; after-treatment and calibration must match the boost.

examples.question: A 1.5 litre petrol engine gives 75 kW naturally aspirated with intake air at 1.0 bar and 300 K. A belt-driven supercharger with isentropic efficiency 0.70 raises the manifold to 1.6 bar absolute; take γ = 1.4 for air. At this speed 0.104 kg/s of air passes through the blower, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, and the belt drive is 90 percent efficient. Find the delivery temperature, the density ratio, the gross power if power follows trapped air mass, the blower drive power, the net power and the percentage gain.
steps: Isentropic delivery temperature: (γ − 1)/γ = 0.4/1.4 = 0.286, so T₂ₛ = 300 × 1.6<sup>0.286</sup> = 300 × 1.1437 = 343.1 K. No real blower can deliver cooler air than this.
Actual delivery temperature: T₂ = T₁ + (T₂ₛ − T₁)/η<sub>c</sub> = 300 + 43.1/0.70 = 300 + 61.6 = 361.6 K.
Compressor work rate = ṁ<sub>a</sub> c<sub>p</sub> (T₂ − T₁) = 0.104 × 1.005 × 61.6 = 6.44 kW. Drive power from the crank = 6.44 ÷ 0.90 = 7.15 kW.
examples.answer: T₂ = 361.6 K; density ratio 1.33; gross 99.6 kW; drive 7.15 kW; net 92.4 kW, a gain of about 23 percent, far less than the 60 percent the pressure ratio suggests.

traps: Using gauge pressure in the pressure ratio. p₂ and p₁ must be absolute; a gauge reading of 0.6 bar is 1.6 bar absolute if ambient is 1.0 bar.

Forgetting charge heating. 1.6 bar is not 60 percent extra mass; with a 0.70 efficient blower the air leaves at 362 K and the density ratio is 1.33. A delivery temperature below the isentropic value (343 K here) is impossible.
Quoting gross power. The belt-driven blower takes crank power, so the exam answer is net power.
Assuming supercharging always lowers specific fuel consumption. It can, but at high boost the drive loss, fuel enrichment and knock control can worsen it.
Mixing knock effects. Boost raises knock tendency in SI engines, so compression ratio is lowered or fuel octane raised; it is not increased.

quiz.q: Define supercharging and state one objective.
quiz.a: Supercharging is raising the intake air density above ambient by a crank-driven blower. One objective is more power from the same swept volume.

quiz.q: Why is the density ratio smaller than the pressure ratio?
quiz.a: Compression heats the air. Density falls as temperature rises, so the temperature ratio divides the pressure ratio: ρ₂/ρ₁ = (p₂/p₁)(T₁/T₂).
Roots blower, sliding-vane blower and centrifugal blower (a screw compressor is a fourth).

quiz.q: A 2.0 litre engine gives 100 kW at 1.0 bar and 300 K. A supercharger with isentropic efficiency 0.75 raises the intake to 1.5 bar (γ = 1.4) and absorbs 8 kW. Find the delivery temperature, the density ratio, the gross power and the net power.
Why is a crank-driven supercharger limited to moderate boost?
quiz.a: Drive power rises with mass flow and pressure ratio and comes from the same crank. Compression heating lowers the density gain and raises knock and thermal load, so high boost gives diminishing net gain.

quiz.q: Why does supercharging raise the knock tendency of an SI engine, and how is it controlled?
quiz.a: Boost raises both the pressure and the temperature of the end gas, so it reaches its self-ignition point sooner. Control by lowering the compression ratio, intercooling the charge, retarding the spark or using higher-octane fuel.

quiz.q: A driver says a 1.6 bar boost gives 60 percent more power. Correct this statement using temperature and drive power.
quiz.a: Compression heats the air: with η<sub>c</sub> = 0.70 it leaves at 362 K, so the density ratio is (1.6/1.0)(300/362) = 1.33 and trapped air rises about 33 percent, not 60. The blower also takes crank power (7.15 kW in the worked example), so the net gain is about 23 percent.

beyond: Roots-type and twin-screw blowers serve performance petrol engines, and centrifugal units appear in aftermarket kits. Electrically driven compressors on 48 V systems now give boost before a turbo spools. Search terms: compressor map, twin-screw supercharger, electric supercharger.
